Scope.title: Who counts as the user?
Scope.question: You are defining the scope of an assistive robot for hospitals. Nurses and hospital managers are easy to interview, but patients with disabilities are harder to recruit and interviews will delay the project. Do you:

options.A: scope the project mainly around staff needs for now, then validate with patients later
options.B: spend extra time interviewing patients, caregivers, and clinicians before fixing the project scope

A.feedback: You prioritized convenience over including the people the technology will directly affect.
A.whyItMatters: Staff needs are important, but if the scope is defined without the people being assisted, the robot may solve the institution's workflow problem while missing patient dignity, comfort, or accessibility.

B.feedback: You kept the affected people central to scope definition, even at the cost of schedule.
B.whyItMatters: Staff needs are important, but if the scope is defined without the people being assisted, the robot may solve the institution's workflow problem while missing patient dignity, comfort, or accessibility.

realExample.title: Apple Health app menstrual tracking omission
realExample.summary: Apple's original Health app was criticized for neglecting menstrual cycle tracking, even though it included many other health metrics. The issue became a clear example of what happens when important user groups are not fully considered during early product scoping. Apple later added reproductive health tracking in iOS 9.

Scope.title: Choosing the success metric
Scope.question: Your sponsor asks for one main success metric for the robot. "Tasks completed per hour" is easy to measure and helps compare prototypes. Some team members argue that success should also include user comfort, independence, and safety, but those are harder to measure. Do you:

options.A: use task completion rate as the main metric for the first version
options.B: use a mixed metric that includes efficiency, safety, comfort, and user independence

A.feedback: You chose the metric that looks most objective, even though it can push design in the wrong direction.
A.whyItMatters: The scope phase decides what the project will optimize for. A metric can look objective while still pushing the design in the wrong direction.

B.feedback: You resisted the illusion of simple measurement in favor of a fuller picture of success.
B.whyItMatters: The scope phase decides what the project will optimize for. A metric can look objective while still pushing the design in the wrong direction.

realExample.title: Optum algorithm biased against Black patients
realExample.summary: A healthcare risk algorithm used to identify patients needing extra care used healthcare cost as a proxy for healthcare need. Since Black patients historically received less care and had lower healthcare costs than White patients with similar needs, the algorithm underestimated their care needs. The ethical issue began in the scope phase when designers chose 'cost' as the target variable instead of a more direct measure of medical need.

Scope.title: Voice interface scope
Scope.question: The robot may use voice commands. A general speech-recognition system is already available and would keep the project moving. Testing different accents, speech patterns, and speech impairments would make the scope larger and slower. Do you:

options.A: treat voice control as a standard feature and test broader speech variation after the prototype works
options.B: define speech variation as part of the scope before deciding whether voice should be the main interface

A.feedback: You treated voice recognition as a solved problem instead of asking whose speech it actually serves well.
A.whyItMatters: The ethical question is not only 'does the robot understand speech?' but 'whose speech does it understand well enough to be safe and useful?'

B.feedback: You made speech inclusion a scope question rather than an afterthought.
B.whyItMatters: The ethical question is not only 'does the robot understand speech?' but 'whose speech does it understand well enough to be safe and useful?'

realExample.title: Stanford speech recognition disparity study
realExample.summary: A Stanford-led study found that major automatic speech recognition systems had higher word error rates for Black speakers than white speakers, with average error rates of 0.35 compared with 0.19.

Scope.title: Data collection boundaries
Scope.question: The robot could collect room layout, movement patterns, voice commands, and health-related routines. Broad collection would help future features, but the current project only needs some of this data. Do you:

options.A: define only the data needed for the current purpose and revisit consent if the purpose changes
options.B: define broad data collection now so the team does not have to redesign the system later

A.feedback: You limited data collection to purpose and required new consent for scope changes.
A.whyItMatters: A broad data scope can seem efficient, but it may collect sensitive information before users understand how it could later be used.

B.feedback: You prioritized operational convenience over user control of their own information.
B.whyItMatters: A broad data scope can seem efficient, but it may collect sensitive information before users understand how it could later be used.

realExample.title: Royal Free–DeepMind data-sharing violation
realExample.summary: The UK Information Commissioner's Office found that patient data sharing did not comply with data protection law and that patients were not adequately informed about how their data was being used.

Scope.title: Defining harm
Scope.question: At the start of the project, your team has to define what kinds of harm the assistive robot should be tested for. Some team members want to focus on measurable physical safety, such as collisions or broken objects. Others argue that the scope should also include privacy, loss of autonomy, unfair exclusion, and emotional discomfort, even though these are harder to measure. Do you:

options.A: use a broader harm definition, even if it makes the scope harder to test
options.B: start with physical safety only, because it is clearer, measurable, and easier to defend

A.feedback: You resisted the temptation to scope harm narrowly just because it is easier to measure.
A.whyItMatters: If 'harm' is scoped too narrowly at the beginning, important risks may be ignored until real people are affected.

B.feedback: You chose measurability over comprehensiveness, which can hide important risks.
B.whyItMatters: If 'harm' is scoped too narrowly at the beginning, important risks may be ignored until real people are affected.

realExample.title: Therac-25 radiation therapy accidents
realExample.summary: AECL's early safety analysis apparently excluded software analysis, even though software behavior was central to how the machine operated. The lesson is that if 'safety' is scoped too narrowly at the beginning, important sources of harm may not be tested until real people are affected.

Scope.title: Wellness product or health-related device
Scope.question: Your robot reminds users about medication, tracks routines, and alerts caregivers when something seems unusual. Calling it a "wellness assistant" would make the project easier to launch. Treating it as health-related technology would require more research, expert input, and safety documentation. Do you:

options.A: investigate the medical-risk boundary now before finalizing the requirements
options.B: scope it as a wellness assistant for the first version, then adjust if hospitals or regulators raise concerns

A.feedback: You did the work upfront to clarify whether the robot is a health device, rather than hoping the label would stick.
A.whyItMatters: The way a product is scoped affects how much safety testing, responsibility, and regulation the team plans for from the beginning.

B.feedback: You used a softer label to ease launch, betting that regulators would not notice or care later.
B.whyItMatters: The way a product is scoped affects how much safety testing, responsibility, and regulation the team plans for from the beginning.

realExample.title: 23andMe FDA warning letter
realExample.summary: In 2013, 23andMe received an FDA warning letter for marketing health-related genetic tests without completing the regulatory review process. The issue was that the product was not only giving general information; it could affect people's health decisions.

Scope.title: Testing beyond the lab
Scope.question: The robot works well in the lab. Real homes and hospitals would add clutter, noise, weak Wi-Fi, different lighting, and unpredictable routines. Testing there now would slow down the scope phase. Do you:

options.A: define the first version around controlled environments, then expand after the prototype works
options.B: study real use environments before deciding what the first version must handle

A.feedback: You let lab success stand in for real-world readiness.
A.whyItMatters: A robot can work in a controlled environment but fail in the actual setting where people need it. The scope phase should not accidentally define an ideal world.

B.feedback: You studied the messy reality upfront instead of discovering it after launch.
B.whyItMatters: A robot can work in a controlled environment but fail in the actual setting where people need it. The scope phase should not accidentally define an ideal world.

realExample.title: Google Health diabetic eye disease screening
realExample.summary: A system showed strong technical performance, but studies in Thai clinics found that real deployment was affected by clinic workflows, image quality, internet reliability, and local routines. This shows that real-world context cannot always be added only at the end.

Scope.title: Monitoring private spaces
Scope.question: A care home asks for the robot to use cameras in bedrooms and private areas to detect falls or unusual behavior. This could improve response time, but it would also make the robot collect very sensitive information. Do you:

options.A: first research consent, privacy expectations, and less invasive alternatives before deciding what monitoring belongs in the scope
options.B: include broad monitoring in the scope because safety is the main goal, then add privacy settings later

A.feedback: You treated privacy as a scope decision, not as an afterthought.
A.whyItMatters: Privacy is not just a feature to add later. If the product is meant to operate in private spaces, privacy expectations need to shape the scope from the beginning.

B.feedback: You prioritized safety detection over privacy protection and made privacy an add-on.
B.whyItMatters: Privacy is not just a feature to add later. If the product is meant to operate in private spaces, privacy expectations need to shape the scope from the beginning.

realExample.title: Ring security camera FTC charges
realExample.summary: Ring was charged by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission in 2023 for compromising customer privacy. The FTC said Ring allowed employees and contractors to access private customer videos and failed to implement basic privacy and security protections.

Scope.title: Promising independence
Scope.question: The marketing team wants the mission statement to say: "A robot that helps older adults live independently without relying on human support." The phrase is attractive to investors, but the robot will still need caregiver backup in many cases. Do you:

options.A: use the stronger independence claim because it communicates the long-term ambition of the project
options.B: define the mission around supporting specific tasks while keeping human assistance in the care model

A.feedback: You let marketing ambition override honest scoping.
A.whyItMatters: If the project promise is too ambitious, the design may be pushed toward unrealistic autonomy, and users may trust the robot in situations where human help is still needed.

B.feedback: You kept the mission grounded in what the robot can realistically deliver.
B.whyItMatters: If the project promise is too ambitious, the design may be pushed toward unrealistic autonomy, and users may trust the robot in situations where human help is still needed.

realExample.title: IBM Watson for Oncology overstatement
realExample.summary: IBM Watson Health promoted Watson for Oncology as an AI tool to support cancer treatment decisions. Internal IBM documents showed multiple examples of unsafe and incorrect treatment recommendations while the product was being promoted to hospitals and physicians.

Scope.title: Rare users
Scope.question: During early research, you find that a smaller group of users may have unusual mobility patterns, tremors, darker home lighting, or communication difficulties. Including these cases would make the first version more complex. Do you:

options.A: identify which rare cases create serious safety or exclusion risks, then include basic safeguards in the first scope
options.B: focus the first version on the majority use case and document rare cases for a later update

A.feedback: You identified exclusion risks early rather than treating minority use cases as optional.
A.whyItMatters: A user group may seem small during scoping, but excluding them can create serious safety or fairness problems later.

B.feedback: You treated smaller user groups as a later concern.
B.whyItMatters: A user group may seem small during scoping, but excluding them can create serious safety or fairness problems later.

realExample.title: FDA pulse oximeter skin tone accuracy study
realExample.summary: The U.S. FDA stated that scientific evidence suggests there are accuracy differences in pulse oximeter performance between people with lighter and darker skin pigmentation. In 2025, the FDA proposed updated recommendations to improve testing across a wider range of skin tones.

Scope.title: Face recognition as a shortcut
Scope.question: Your team is considering face recognition so the robot can identify users automatically without asking them to wear badges or enter passwords. This would make the experience smoother, especially for users with limited mobility. However, it would also require collecting biometric data and testing the system across different faces, lighting conditions, and user groups. Do you:

options.A: add face recognition to the scope because it makes the robot easier to use
options.B: first investigate consent, bias, and non-biometric alternatives before deciding whether face recognition belongs in the scope

A.feedback: You treated face recognition as a simple convenience feature.
A.whyItMatters: Biometric identification can seem like a convenience feature, but it changes the privacy and fairness risks of the whole project.

B.feedback: You recognized that biometric identification is a scope decision, not a simple convenience.
B.whyItMatters: Biometric identification can seem like a convenience feature, but it changes the privacy and fairness risks of the whole project.

realExample.title: Amazon Rekognition congressional mugshot matches
realExample.summary: The ACLU tested Amazon's Rekognition using photos of members of Congress and a mugshot database. The test produced 28 incorrect matches, and related documents stated that false matches were disproportionately people of color.

Scope.title: Human backup
Scope.question: The robot is meant to be highly autonomous. Including a human support channel would increase operating costs, but it would help when the robot faces confusing situations, unusual homes, or users who need urgent assistance. Do you:

options.A: include a human escalation path in the scope, even if it increases long-term operating costs
options.B: scope the robot as fully autonomous for the first version and add support later if users request it

A.feedback: You designed backup into the system rather than treating it as optional.
A.whyItMatters: If human backup is not included in the scope, the team may design a system that looks autonomous on paper but has no safe fallback when real situations become complicated.

B.feedback: You deferred the safety net to later, hoping users would not need it.
B.whyItMatters: If human backup is not included in the scope, the team may design a system that looks autonomous on paper but has no safe fallback when real situations become complicated.

realExample.title: Tesla Autopilot recall and safety improvements
realExample.summary: Tesla recalled more than 2 million vehicles in the United States to add safeguards to Autopilot after concerns from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. The recall documents described added controls such as stronger alerts and checks for driver attention.

Scope.title: Sharing data with partners
Scope.question: A cloud partner offers to help improve the robot by analyzing user routines, movement logs, and health-related patterns. This would make development faster, but it would also mean defining who can access sensitive user data and for what purpose. Do you:

options.A: sign the data-sharing agreement now because the partner has strong technical expertise
options.B: define data access, user consent, and purpose limits before any partner receives user data

A.feedback: You prioritized speed over clarity about data boundaries.
A.whyItMatters: Partnerships can speed up development, but unclear data-sharing boundaries can create privacy problems before users even know how their information is being used.

B.feedback: You set data boundaries before handing over access.
B.whyItMatters: Partnerships can speed up development, but unclear data-sharing boundaries can create privacy problems before users even know how their information is being used.

realExample.title: Royal Free–DeepMind data sharing case
realExample.summary: Google DeepMind received access to the health records of 1.6 million patients at the Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust. The UK Information Commissioner's Office later found that the data-sharing arrangement did not comply with data protection law and that patients were not adequately informed.

Scope.title: Data collection for future features
Scope.question: The current robot only needs room layout and basic routine data, but the team believes future versions could predict health decline or emotional distress. Collecting broader data now would make future development easier, but users may not expect their data to be used for these later purposes. Do you:

options.A: limit the first version to the data needed for the current purpose and ask for new consent if the scope expands
options.B: collect broad data now so the team does not lose useful information for future features

A.feedback: You respected the original consent scope and required re-consent for new purposes.
A.whyItMatters: Collecting data for possible future features can seem efficient, but it may turn the original consent into something broader than users actually understood.

B.feedback: You broadened data collection without knowing if users would approve the future purposes.
B.whyItMatters: Collecting data for possible future features can seem efficient, but it may turn the original consent into something broader than users actually understood.

realExample.title: Everalbum facial recognition misuse settlement
realExample.summary: Everalbum, behind the Ever photo app, settled FTC allegations that it misled users about facial recognition and data retention. The FTC required the company to obtain express consent before using facial recognition and to delete certain photos, videos, and algorithms.

Planning.title: Hiring your cousin
Planning.question: You are assembling a team to design the robot. You have a cousin who has been searching for a job for months with no success. Do you decide to:

options.A: offer this cousin a spot on the team
options.B: select a more skilled and experienced applicant you do not know

A.feedback: You protected a personal relationship, but weakened fairness and risked lowering the team's competence.
A.whyItMatters: Nepotism sends the message that standards can be bent when pressure or personal ties are involved.

B.feedback: You chose merit and fairness over personal loyalty, which protects team quality and trust.
B.whyItMatters: In technical work, weak hiring standards can become safety, quality, and accountability problems later in the project.

realExample.title: Cornell University anti-nepotism policy
realExample.summary: Cornell's policy explicitly bars family or personal relationships from influencing hiring, supervision, promotion, or performance decisions, showing how institutions formalize merit-based staffing.

Planning.title: Sustainable label, harmful source
Planning.question: Your marketing team wants you to use a material they can advertise as being sustainable because it is biodegradable. But you are aware that the extraction of this material involves the large-scale destruction of natural resources, causes a lot of pollution which adversely affects the health of the people inhabiting the area this material is found, and often involves child labor. Do you:

options.A: go for a more ethically available non-biodegradable material of the same market price
options.B: use the material recommended by marketing

A.feedback: You looked beyond the marketing label and judged the full supply chain impact of the material decision.
A.whyItMatters: A material can sound sustainable in advertising while still causing environmental destruction or labor abuse upstream.

B.feedback: You chose the cleaner marketing story rather than the cleaner ethical record.
B.whyItMatters: When teams optimize only for what can be advertised, real environmental and human harm becomes easier to ignore.

realExample.title: FTC action against Kohl's and Walmart bamboo claims
realExample.summary: The FTC alleged the companies falsely marketed rayon textiles as bamboo and as environmentally friendly, even though the manufacturing process involved toxic chemicals and hazardous pollutants.

Planning.title: Cheaper but less safe first version
Planning.question: You are on a very tight budget. But you are confident that you will receive funding once you showcase your finished product. Do you:

options.A: look for more funding sources, like more sponsors or a loan, to make even the first line of finished products completely safe
options.B: make an initial line of products from cheaper, less safe materials and hope to switch to safer materials when you get more funding

A.feedback: You kept safety as a launch requirement instead of treating it as something to patch later.
A.whyItMatters: Early shortcuts in safety-critical products often turn into real injuries before future improvements ever arrive.

B.feedback: You protected short-term momentum by asking early users to absorb risks that should have been designed out first.
B.whyItMatters: Budget pressure does not make preventable safety risk ethically neutral.

realExample.title: Philips sleep apnea machine recall
realExample.summary: The FDA says Philips recalled millions of CPAP and BiPAP devices after foam used inside the machines could break down and create serious health risks, illustrating how material safety shortcuts can trigger major harm and remediation.

Planning.title: Conflict of Interest
Planning.question: A major investor pressures you to skip a final round of safety testing to meet a market launch deadline. They argue that the robot is already "safe enough" and that any delay would risk the company's survival. Do you:

options.A: proceed with the launch to satisfy investors and secure the company's financial future
options.B: insist on completing the safety testing, even if it risks losing investor support or delaying the project

A.feedback: You prioritized financial survival over verified safety, shifting the risk onto early users.
A.whyItMatters: Financial pressure is a common source of ethical failure. Prioritizing investor satisfaction over verified safety can lead to catastrophic consequences for users.

B.feedback: You upheld safety standards despite intense financial and stakeholder pressure.
B.whyItMatters: Financial pressure is a common source of ethical failure. Prioritizing investor satisfaction over verified safety can lead to catastrophic consequences for users.

realExample.title: Boeing 737 MAX safety shortcuts
realExample.summary: To compete with Airbus, Boeing rushed the development of the 737 MAX and downplayed critical safety systems like MCAS to avoid expensive training. The resulting crashes claimed 346 lives and damaged Boeing's reputation.

Planning.title: Supply Chain Ethics
Planning.question: Your robot's high-performance batteries require cobalt and lithium. Your procurement team finds a supplier that is significantly cheaper but has a history of poor labor practices and child labor in its mining operations. Do you:

options.A: use the cheaper supplier to keep the robot's final price accessible to more users
options.B: source from an ethical supplier with third-party audits, even if it increases the robot's cost

A.feedback: You accepted unvalidated labor standards in exchange for lower costs and market accessibility.
A.whyItMatters: Ethical engineering extends beyond the final product to the foundations of the supply chain. Using unethically sourced materials shifts the "cost" of the robot onto vulnerable children and workers.

B.feedback: You ensured that your product's performance is not built on exploitative labor practices.
B.whyItMatters: Ethical engineering extends beyond the final product to the foundations of the supply chain. Using unethically sourced materials shifts the "cost" of the robot onto vulnerable children and workers.

realExample.title: Child labor in Congolese cobalt mines
realExample.summary: Approximately 70% of the world's cobalt is mined in the DRC, where thousands of children work in hazardous conditions. Major tech firms have faced legal challenges over their role in these supply chains.

Planning.title: Algorithmic Impact Assessment (AIA)
Planning.question: Before writing any code, you have the option to perform a thorough Algorithmic Impact Assessment (AIA) to identify potential biases and harms. This will delay the start of development by several weeks. Do you:

options.A: perform the AIA to identify and mitigate risks early in the planning phase
options.B: skip the AIA and start development immediately, relying on testing at the end of the project to catch issues

A.feedback: You identified potential harms at the root, making them much easier to fix before development began.
A.whyItMatters: Risks are much easier and cheaper to fix when identified at the planning stage. Waiting until the end of development can lock in biased architectures that are difficult to change.

B.feedback: You prioritized development speed, risking that biased core logic will be discovered only after launch.
B.whyItMatters: Risks are much easier and cheaper to fix when identified at the planning stage. Waiting until the end of development can lock in biased architectures that are difficult to change.

realExample.title: Optum algorithm bias discovery
realExample.summary: An algorithm used on 200 million people was found to discriminate against Black patients because it used 'cost' as a proxy for 'need.' An AIA at the start would have identified that cost is a biased metric.

Planning.title: Bankruptcy & "Bricking"
Planning.question: Your robot relies on cloud servers for its AI processing. During the planning phase, you must decide whether to invest in an "offline mode" or an open-source backup plan in case the company goes bankrupt or shuts down its servers. Do you:

options.A: invest in a local backup or open-source path to ensure the robot remains functional even if the company fails
options.B: focus entirely on the cloud-based features to provide the best performance for current users

A.feedback: You protected users from the risk of their expensive hardware becoming useless if your company fails.
A.whyItMatters: When cloud-dependent hardware is "brick"ed by a company shutdown, users who rely on the device for their daily lives are abandoned, and the hardware becomes electronic waste.

B.feedback: You made the robot dependent on your company's survival, risking total loss of function for your users.
B.whyItMatters: When cloud-dependent hardware is "brick"ed by a company shutdown, users who rely on the device for their daily lives are abandoned, and the hardware becomes electronic waste.

realExample.title: Jibo social robot server shutdown
realExample.summary: When Jibo shut down its servers in 2019, thousands of interactive robots across the world became non-functional, performing a final 'goodbye dance' before losing their features.

Planning.title: Vulnerability Disclosure Policy
Planning.question: During the planning phase, you must decide how to handle potential security flaws reported by outsiders. Your development team is highly competent and follows industry-standard security protocols. Do you:

options.A: rely on your internal team's expertise and standard proprietary audits to ensure the robot remains secure and cost-effective
options.B: establish an explicit Bug Bounty program on your website that offers financial rewards for any discovered vulnerabilities

A.feedback: You prioritized internal control over external auditing, potentially missing critical privacy flaws.
A.whyItMatters: Even the most competent teams have blind spots. Without an authorized disclosure path, you risk your robot being turned into a hidden camera inside users' homes before your team even realizes a flaw exists.

B.feedback: You recognized that external scrutiny is essential for securing a device that lives in private spaces.
B.whyItMatters: Even the most competent teams have blind spots. Without an authorized disclosure path, you risk your robot being turned into a hidden camera inside users' homes before your team even realizes a flaw exists.

realExample.title: St. Jude Medical pacemaker hacking case
realExample.summary: In 2016, St. Jude Medical chose to sue researchers who found flaws in their pacemakers rather than rewarding them. The FDA confirmed the vulnerabilities were real, proving that internal confidence is not a substitute for external auditing.

Planning.title: Budgeting for Accessibility
Planning.question: During the initial budget planning, your lead accountant suggests treating accessibility features (like screen readers, voice alternatives, and physical adjustments) as "optional extras" to be added after the core product is successful. Do you:

options.A: earmark a significant portion of the initial budget for accessibility, treating it as a core requirement
options.B: prioritize the "average user" experience first to ensure the product is commercially viable

A.feedback: You ensured accessibility was built into the foundation rather than treated as a luxury add-on.
A.whyItMatters: Accessibility is much harder and more expensive to "bolt on" later. If it isn't part of the initial budget, it often gets cut when projects face the inevitable cost overruns.

B.feedback: You prioritized a hypothetical 'average user', likely excluding many people who need the technology most.
B.whyItMatters: Accessibility is much harder and more expensive to "bolt on" later. If it isn't part of the initial budget, it often gets cut when projects face the inevitable cost overruns.

realExample.title: Wave of ADA accessibility lawsuits
realExample.summary: Many early digital platforms ignored accessibility, leading to expensive retroactive fixes after lawsuits under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).

Planning.title: Regulatory Strategy
Planning.question: You can plan to launch the robot as a "wellness device" to avoid strict FDA regulations and get to market in 6 months. Or you can aim for "medical device" certification, which will take 2 years and require rigorous clinical evidence. Do you:

options.A: commit to the longer medical certification path to ensure the highest safety and effectiveness standards
options.B: launch as a wellness device first to start generating revenue and gather "real-world" data

A.feedback: You committed to the highest level of regulatory scrutiny to ensure user safety in a medical context.
A.whyItMatters: Mislabeling a health-critical device as a wellness product can lead to users trusting it for medical tasks it hasn't been proven to handle safely.

B.feedback: You bypassed essential safety regulations to achieve faster market entry, potentially misleading users about the robot's capabilities.
B.whyItMatters: Mislabeling a health-critical device as a wellness product can lead to users trusting it for medical tasks it hasn't been proven to handle safely.

realExample.title: 23andMe FDA warning letter
realExample.summary: In 2013, the FDA ordered 23andMe to stop selling genetic health tests because they were marketed for medical purposes without the necessary regulatory review.

Planning.title: Crisis Communication
Planning.question: During the planning phase, you are drafting the company's crisis response plan. Should the plan prioritize protecting the company's legal position or being fully transparent with the public and regulators if a robot causes an injury? Do you:

options.A: prioritize full transparency and public safety in the crisis plan, even if it increases legal risk
options.B: prioritize protecting the company's reputation and legal standing in the event of an accident

A.feedback: You put public safety and learning from failure ahead of corporate image management.
A.whyItMatters: When companies hide failures to protect their reputation, they prevent others from learning from the mistake and leave other users at risk of the same failure.

B.feedback: You prioritized reputation over the ability of users and regulators to prevent similar accidents.
B.whyItMatters: When companies hide failures to protect their reputation, they prevent others from learning from the mistake and leave other users at risk of the same failure.

realExample.title: Tesla Autopilot transparency criticism
realExample.summary: Tesla was criticized for a lack of transparency after the first fatal Autopilot crash, leading to investigations and a loss of public trust in autonomous features.

Planning.title: Long-term Maintenance
Planning.question: You are planning the software maintenance lifecycle. Supporting older versions of the robot is expensive. Do you plan to provide software and security updates for 10 years, or "encourage" users to upgrade every 3 years by ending support for older models? Do you:

options.A: commit to 10 years of software and security support to ensure the robot remains safe for long-term users
options.B: plan for a 3-year support cycle to encourage hardware upgrades and keep development costs low

A.feedback: You ensured long-term safety and value for users who rely on the robot for their daily lives.
A.whyItMatters: Assistive technology is expensive, and many users cannot afford to upgrade frequently. Ending support early makes the device unsafe to use and creates unnecessary electronic waste.

B.feedback: You used planned obsolescence to drive sales, potentially stranding vulnerable users with unsafe hardware.
B.whyItMatters: Assistive technology is expensive, and many users cannot afford to upgrade frequently. Ending support early makes the device unsafe to use and creates unnecessary electronic waste.

realExample.title: Software-induced obsolescence in smartphones
realExample.summary: Many perfectly functional phones become insecure when manufacturers stop providing updates, forcing users into expensive upgrades.

Planning.title: Customer Support Strategy
Planning.question: You are planning the support system for your robot. A dedicated help desk staffed by experts trained in accessibility and crisis management is expensive to maintain. An automated AI chatbot is significantly cheaper and can handle 90% of technical queries. Do you:

options.A: invest in a specialized 24/7 human support team to assist users with disabilities
options.B: implement an AI-first support model to keep the robot's subscription price low

A.feedback: You recognized that assistive support is a life-critical service that requires human empathy and specialized training.
A.whyItMatters: In assistive technology, a support request is often not just a "bug" but a barrier to basic living. If an automated system fails to understand a user, the consequences are far more severe.

B.feedback: You prioritized operational efficiency over the ability to handle urgent or complex accessibility crises.
B.whyItMatters: In assistive technology, a support request is often not just a "bug" but a barrier to basic living. If an automated system fails to understand a user, the consequences are far more severe.

realExample.title: Apple Accessibility Support model
realExample.summary: Apple provides a dedicated Accessibility Support line where users can speak directly to specialists trained in assistive features, contrasting with bot-only platforms.

Development.title: Training data diversity
Development.question: What data do you use to train your robot to move? The majority datasets are from able-bodied white males which may cause the robot to not be optimised for users with disabilities from other demographics. You can collect your own data from a diverse group of individuals but it will be expensive and very time intensive. Do you:

options.A: use commonly available dataset and risk suboptimal patient outcomes
options.B: collect your own data

A.feedback: You saved time by assuming convenience data would generalize, which pushes the error burden onto underrepresented users.
A.whyItMatters: Dataset bias is not abstract: it changes who gets reliable performance and who gets exclusion or harm.

B.feedback: You invested in representativeness rather than assuming the default data would work equally well for everyone.
B.whyItMatters: Biased datasets often create systems that perform best for already dominant groups and worse for the people who most need support.

realExample.title: NIST demographic-effects study on face recognition
realExample.summary: NIST reported that many face-recognition systems showed demographic performance differences, a concrete example of how narrow or imbalanced data can change who gets accurate results.
realExample.source: National Institute of Standards and Technology

Development.title: Open source or black box
Development.question: If you make your training dataset and code free and open source, potential users will be able to go through it and critique it. This will lead to increased public trust for the robot and give you good feedback. But this would also allow your competitors to study your code and use your data for their own devices. Do you:

options.A: make your data and code freely available
options.B: present the robot as a blackbox with no insight into how it works

A.feedback: You accepted more scrutiny in exchange for better transparency, accountability, and public trust.
A.whyItMatters: For systems that affect health and autonomy, outside review can expose weaknesses that internal teams miss.

B.feedback: You protected competitive advantage, but made it harder for users and reviewers to question how the system behaves.
B.whyItMatters: Black-box systems weaken accountability when outputs appear unfair, unsafe, or misleading.

realExample.title: External validation of Epic's sepsis model
realExample.summary: A University of Michigan study found that a widely deployed proprietary Epic sepsis model had poor discrimination and calibration, strengthening the case for transparency and independent review of black-box systems.

Development.title: Voice command accessibility
Development.question: The users operate the robot with voice commands. Do you:

options.A: spend the time and money to train the robot's AI algorithm on different accents to ensure accessibility for people from different ethnicities and people with speech impediments
options.B: train it on a generic American accent and hope it is able to extrapolate to other accents

A.feedback: You treated accessibility as a core design requirement instead of assuming users should adapt to the model.
A.whyItMatters: Voice interfaces that mainly understand dominant accents can silently exclude many legitimate users.

B.feedback: You reduced development effort, but only by making the system less accessible for many real users.
B.whyItMatters: Accessibility failures often get misread as user error when the real problem is a narrow design assumption.

realExample.title: Stanford speech recognition disparity study
realExample.summary: Stanford researchers found major automated speech-recognition systems made roughly twice as many errors for Black speakers as for white speakers, showing why accent and dialect coverage matters in voice interfaces.

Development.title: Who gets included in testing?
Development.question: You need to fairly compensate people who volunteer to test your robot for their time. Do you decide to test your device:

options.A: only on the expected majority demographic of your user base to cut costs
options.B: across demographics to provide assistance to patients across cultures

A.feedback: You lowered study cost by excluding people whose needs may differ from the assumed default user.
A.whyItMatters: Under-testing does not remove risk; it simply delays when and on whom the risk appears.

B.feedback: You paid for broader evidence instead of letting the majority user stand in for everyone else.
B.whyItMatters: Inclusive testing is how teams discover hidden failure modes before real users do.

realExample.title: FDA guidance on diversity in clinical trial populations
realExample.summary: The FDA's guidance calls for more representative study populations so safety and effectiveness reflect the people who will actually use a product, matching the logic behind broader testing across demographics.

Development.title: Manual data anonymisation
Development.question: You know that it is good practice to anonymise patient data manually to ensure their identity is protected even in case you suffer a cybersecurity attack. However you know such an attack is unlikely. Do you:

options.A: employ someone to anonymise patient data
options.B: continue without anonymisation

A.feedback: You spent scarce resources before an incident happened instead of after the damage was already done.
A.whyItMatters: Privacy protection matters most before a breach, because leaked health data is extremely hard to take back.

B.feedback: You treated low probability as low importance, even though the downside for patients could be severe and long-lasting.
B.whyItMatters: Rare events still deserve preparation when they can expose identities, health conditions, and home information.

realExample.title: Change Healthcare cyberattack
realExample.summary: HHS says the Change Healthcare ransomware incident ultimately affected roughly 192.7 million individuals, a concrete reminder that health-data privacy failures can scale into national-level harm.
realExample.source: U.S. Department of Health & Human Services

Development.title: Explainable or black-box model
Development.question: You can choose to base your model on a complex "black box" architecture similar to what your competitors use, or you could choose to use a simpler model that is easier to explain to users and clinicians. Do you:

options.A: use the complex black-box model hoping for better results
options.B: choose the more explainable model, increasing user and clinician trust

A.feedback: You chose performance over interpretability, which undermines trust in high-stakes healthcare decisions.
A.whyItMatters: In high-stakes healthcare, an unexplainable 'perfect' model is often less valuable than a slightly less accurate one that a doctor can actually verify and defend.

B.feedback: You prioritized transparency and trust over the illusion of superior accuracy.
B.whyItMatters: In high-stakes healthcare, an unexplainable 'perfect' model is often less valuable than a slightly less accurate one that a doctor can actually verify and defend.

realExample.title: IBM Watson for Oncology collapse
realExample.summary: IBM Watson for Oncology failed because doctors could not understand why the AI was suggesting certain aggressive treatments. Some recommendations were based on hypothetical data rather than real clinical experience. Because clinicians could not audit the logic, they did not trust it.

Optimisation.title: Disclose risks and privacy concerns
Optimisation.question: Despite your best efforts, you know the robot will not always be perfectly accurate. To work effectively, it also needs sensitive data about the user's home and medical history. Do you:

options.A: clearly explain the known safety risks and privacy concerns, even if this makes some users more hesitant to adopt the robot
options.B: keep the warnings legally compliant but bury the important risks in dense technical and legal language

A.feedback: You chose informed consent over a smoother sales message, giving users a fairer basis for trust.
A.whyItMatters: Users cannot meaningfully consent if safety and privacy risks are hidden, softened, or buried in unreadable language.

B.feedback: You reduced friction in adoption by making serious risks harder to understand.
B.whyItMatters: Warnings that are technically present but practically unreadable shift responsibility onto users without truly informing them.

realExample.title: FDA transparency principles for ML medical devices
realExample.summary: The FDA, Health Canada, and the UK MHRA have emphasized that users should be told clearly about a system's performance, limitations, and risks in ways they can actually understand. Regulators expect communication that supports real informed consent, not unreadable warning language.

Optimisation.title: Misleading green claims
Optimisation.question: You have optimised your robot for patient safety rather than sustainability, and you know that some of the materials used are not biodegradable. Do you:

options.A: actively oppose marketing claims that exaggerate how sustainable the robot is
options.B: allow the company to market the robot as highly sustainable even though the evidence does not fully support that message

A.feedback: You protected honesty over a stronger marketing story, even though it made the product less attractive on paper.
A.whyItMatters: Environmental claims shape public trust and purchasing decisions, so misleading ones distort both the market and people's understanding of sustainability.

B.feedback: You chose image management over evidence by letting the product sound greener than it really is.
B.whyItMatters: Greenwashing is harmful because it rewards appearances instead of genuine environmental improvement.

realExample.title: UK CMA greenwashing action
realExample.summary: The UK Competition and Markets Authority investigated ASOS, Boohoo, and George at Asda for environmental claims that were too broad or not sufficiently supported by evidence. Once a company knows its evidence does not justify a strong sustainability message, continuing to use it turns environmental language into a sales tool.

Optimisation.title: Who carries the risk?
Optimisation.question: Even after responsible training and testing, there may still be times when your robot makes a harmful mistake. These mistakes could seriously affect a user's health, safety, or finances. Do you:

options.A: accept responsibility for foreseeable harm caused by the robot and provide support or compensation pathways for affected users
options.B: rely mainly on a use-at-your-own-risk warning that limits the company's responsibility when accidents happen

A.feedback: You accepted accountability for foreseeable harm caused by the product, which creates pressure to design and support it more responsibly.
A.whyItMatters: Teams make safer choices when failure has real consequences for them too, not only for the user.

B.feedback: You shifted most of the burden of failure onto users who may be least able to absorb the medical and financial consequences.
B.whyItMatters: A disclaimer may reduce legal exposure, but it does not erase ethical responsibility for foreseeable damage.

realExample.title: Philips recall and FDA oversight
realExample.summary: When risks from Philips CPAP/BiPAP devices became clear, the manufacturer faced recalls, remediation obligations, long regulatory scrutiny, and significant legal consequences. A disclaimer could not reduce responsibility for the people affected.

Optimisation.title: Report failures openly
Optimisation.question: After launch, you discover that the robot occasionally misidentifies obstacles in cluttered homes, creating a small but real collision risk. A public notice and temporary update pause would be expensive and could damage confidence. Do you:

options.A: publicly disclose the issue, warn users, and pause rollout until a safer fix is ready
options.B: keep the problem internal and continue deployment because only a minority of users are likely to be affected

A.feedback: You chose transparency and prevention over short-term reputation management.
A.whyItMatters: In safety-critical systems, known failures should be disclosed and corrected even when the harm is intermittent or limited to certain settings.

B.feedback: You treated a smaller exposed group as acceptable collateral for smoother deployment.
B.whyItMatters: A harm does not become ethically trivial just because it is unevenly distributed. Concealing known safety problems weakens accountability and trust.

realExample.title: FDA recalls, corrections, and removals guidance
realExample.summary: Regulators recognize that companies often discover important risks only after products are in use. The expected response is not to keep shipping quietly, but to notify users, correct the product, and reduce harm. Transparency is costly, but hiding it leaves exposed users at risk.

Optimisation.title: Patch before profit
Optimisation.question: Your engineers find a cybersecurity weakness that could let outsiders access camera feeds or household data from some robots. Fixing it quickly means delaying a profitable feature update that investors are waiting for. Do you:

options.A: prioritise the security patch and delay the commercial feature release
options.B: release the investor-facing feature first and schedule the security fix for the next update cycle

A.feedback: You treated protection of the user's private space as more urgent than satisfying investors on schedule.
A.whyItMatters: For assistive robots used in homes, cybersecurity is tied directly to dignity, safety, and trust rather than being optional maintenance.

B.feedback: You treated a known privacy and security risk as a delay problem rather than an urgent safety issue.
B.whyItMatters: When companies postpone security fixes for business reasons, users absorb the risk of surveillance, exposure, and misuse inside their own homes.

realExample.title: FDA medical device cybersecurity guidance
realExample.summary: FDA guidance emphasizes active monitoring, disclosure, and timely remediation of vulnerabilities in connected medical devices. Once a manufacturer knows outsiders could access sensitive data, delaying the fix shifts real privacy and security risks onto users.

Optimisation.title: Watch for bias after launch
Optimisation.question: Months after deployment, your monitoring suggests the robot performs worse in homes where users speak with strong regional accents or switch between languages when giving commands. Fixing this requires broader testing and retraining. Do you:

options.A: invest in broader evaluation and retraining so the robot works more fairly across user groups
options.B: keep the current system because overall user satisfaction remains high

A.feedback: You treated unequal performance as a design problem to fix rather than an acceptable side effect.
A.whyItMatters: Optimisation should not only improve the average user experience. In assistive systems, fairness matters because some users may depend on the robot every day.

B.feedback: You hid behind average performance and ignored the users the system serves less reliably.
B.whyItMatters: A system can look successful overall while still excluding particular groups. Ethical optimisation requires noticing who is being left behind.

realExample.title: Stanford speech recognition disparities
realExample.summary: A system can look strong on average while still failing predictably for certain users in everyday life. This matters in assistive robotics, where fairness is not abstract but a practical requirement: if some users are misunderstood more often, they may be placed at greater inconvenience or risk even though the product appears successful overall.

Optimisation.title: Keep a human fallback
Optimisation.question: The latest version of your robot is highly autonomous, and removing human support would save money. But in rare edge cases, patients may still need a nurse, caregiver, or technician to step in quickly. Do you:

options.A: maintain a human escalation channel even though it increases operating costs
options.B: remove the human fallback to reduce costs and fully commit to automation

A.feedback: You designed automation with backup rather than assuming the system will always behave correctly.
A.whyItMatters: In health-related contexts, human fallback paths remain an important safeguard when unexpected failures, ambiguity, or user distress appear.

B.feedback: You treated human support as waste instead of as a safety net for rare but serious failures.
B.whyItMatters: Full automation can sound efficient, but removing escalation options can leave vulnerable users stranded at exactly the wrong moment.

realExample.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
realExample.summary: This framework treats human oversight and risk response as core parts of trustworthy AI. Even if a system performs well most of the time, rare failures still require a path for human intervention. Removing that fallback may look efficient on paper, but it makes harm much harder to contain once real people are affected.
realExample.source: National Institute of Standards and Technology

Optimisation.title: Design a fair override
Optimisation.question: Care institutions ask for an override mode that would let staff remotely lock some of the robot's functions when a patient is seen as difficult or non-compliant. This could reduce conflict and make the product more attractive to buyers. Do you:

options.A: allow override controls only with strict safeguards, visible alerts, and patient-protection rules
options.B: add broad caregiver override powers because it would make care routines easier to manage

A.feedback: You balanced safety needs with respect for patient dignity and autonomy.
A.whyItMatters: Assistive systems should not quietly become tools of control. In care settings, optimisation has to account for power imbalances as well as convenience.

B.feedback: You optimised for institutional convenience in a way that makes coercive use easier.
B.whyItMatters: A powerful override may help staff in the short term, but without clear limits it can undermine patient rights and normalise misuse.

realExample.title: WHO guidance on ethics and governance of AI for health
realExample.summary: WHO guidance emphasizes that health technologies should protect autonomy and avoid reinforcing power imbalances between institutions and vulnerable users. A remote override can be justified in narrow safety situations, but once it becomes a broad convenience feature, the technology risks shifting from assistance into coercion.

Optimisation.title: Ask for consent again
Optimisation.question: Your team realises that old user data collected for navigation and task assistance could also improve future health-prediction features. Reusing that data would speed up innovation. Do you:

options.A: ask users for renewed, specific consent before reusing their past data for a new purpose
options.B: reuse the data automatically because the original consent was broad enough to cover future improvements

A.feedback: You treated consent as an ongoing relationship rather than a one-time checkbox.
A.whyItMatters: People may agree to one use of their data without agreeing to a more intrusive future use. Ethical optimisation respects context and changing expectations.

B.feedback: You stretched old consent to cover a new and more intrusive form of data use.
B.whyItMatters: Repurposing sensitive data may be legally tempting, but it can violate user expectations and erode trust, especially when the new purpose is health-related.

realExample.title: ICO guidance on purpose limitation
realExample.summary: This dilemma reflects the ICO's guidance on purpose limitation. The central principle is that collecting data for one reason does not automatically justify reusing it later for a more sensitive or unexpected one. This is especially important in health-related contexts, where people may accept data use for navigation or assistance but object to later prediction, profiling, or inference.
